\chapter{How}
\label{ch:la-how}
\hlchaptermodality{26}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can ask how in Latin with quōmodo, and trace it into cómo, come, and comment.}

Say quōmodo, split it into quō and modō, and show how comment double-marks the manner that come and cómo mark once.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[quōmodo]{quōmodo — the real word behind \textquotedblleft{}how,\textquotedblright{} in three Romance languages at once}

\label{lesson:LA-C26-quomodo}



\begin{quote}
You've already met \emph{quōmodo} once, as part of a phrase that turned out \textbf{not} to be classically attested. This lesson is honest about the flip side: the \textbf{word itself} is completely genuine.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: quōmodo — genuinely classical, \textquotedblleft{}by what manner\textquotedblright{}}
\textbf{Quōmodo} (\textquotedblleft{}\textbf{how, in what way}\textquotedblright{}) is a real, common Classical Latin word — a fusion of \textbf{quō} (ablative of \emph{quis/quid}, \textquotedblleft{}what\textquotedblright{}) + \textbf{modō} (ablative of \emph{modus}, \textquotedblleft{}manner, measure\textquotedblright{}), literally \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{by what manner}.\textquotedblright{} It's attested in both \textbf{Cicero} (\emph{Dē Inventiōne}) and \textbf{Seneca} (\emph{Epistulae Mōrālēs}) — genuinely classical, unlike the specific \emph{quōmodo tē habēs?} greeting from Chapter 19, which was a modern construction. The \textbf{word} is real; it was only that one \textbf{exact phrase} that wasn't.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{Quōmodo} is the \textbf{direct source} of Italian's \textbf{come} and Spanish's \textbf{cómo} — both simply continue \emph{quōmodo}, worn down by ordinary sound change.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{cousinweb}
Here's the honest surprise: French's \textbf{comment} is \textbf{not} a simple continuation of \emph{quōmodo} the way Italian and Spanish's words are. French's \textbf{comme} (\textquotedblleft{}how, as, like\textquotedblright{}) continues \emph{quōmodo} just like Italian's \emph{come} does — but then \textbf{comment} picks up French's own \textbf{-ment} adverb ending on top of that, from \textbf{mente} (ablative of \emph{mēns}, \textquotedblleft{}mind\textquotedblright{}) — the \textbf{same} \emph{-ment} that turns any adjective into an adverb (\emph{rapide} $\to$ \emph{rapidement}, \textquotedblleft{}quickly\textquotedblright{}). One well-attested account of this history holds that \emph{comment} therefore marks \textquotedblleft{}manner\textquotedblright{} \textbf{twice} — once via \emph{quōmodo}'s own \emph{modō}, once via \emph{-ment}'s \emph{mente} — where Italian and Spanish mark it only once, though the exact historical steps have more than one scholarly account.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}quōmodo\textquotedblright{} — \textquotedblleft{}how,\textquotedblright{} genuinely classical
  \item quō (what) + modō (manner) — \textquotedblleft{}by what manner\textquotedblright{}
  \item the honest surprise — French's comment double-marks \textquotedblleft{}manner\textquotedblright{}; Italian/Spanish's come/cómo mark it once
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Is \textbf{quōmodo} itself genuinely classical, even though the specific phrase \emph{quōmodo tē habēs?} wasn't? (\textbf{Yes} — the word is real, attested in Cicero and Seneca; only that one specific greeting was modern.) What are quōmodo's two Latin pieces, and what do they mean? (\textbf{Quō} \textquotedblleft{}what\textquotedblright{} + \textbf{modō} \textquotedblleft{}manner\textquotedblright{} — \textquotedblleft{}by what manner.\textquotedblright{}) Is French's \textbf{comment} a simple continuation of \emph{quōmodo}, the way Italian's \emph{come} is? (\textbf{No} — it adds a second \textquotedblleft{}manner\textquotedblright{} marker, \emph{mente}, doubling up where Italian/Spanish only carry the sense once.)
\end{tcolorbox}
